
# Bivariate Distributions
***

Earlier chapters summarized one variable at a time.
We now study two variables together.
Throughout, the data for each observation are grouped together as a vector $(\hat{x}_{i}, \hat{y}_{i})$.
As in [Summary Statistics](01_03_SummaryStatistics.qmd#mean-and-variance), $\hat{x}$ and $\hat{y}$ without a subscript denote all $n$ observed values of each variable.

This chapter asks two questions.

* How often does each combination of values occur?
    * *Joint and marginal distributions*: the joint distribution $\hat{p}(x,y)$ is a table of shares, one per combination of values.
      Summing it over one variable gives the marginal distribution of the other.
    * *Scatterplot*: this shows the joint distribution of continuous data, with one point per observation.
* How does the distribution of $\hat{y}$ change with $\hat{x}$?
    * *Conditional distribution*: this rescales the joint distribution so each row sums to one, $\hat{p}(y \mid x)=\hat{p}(x,y)/\hat{p}(x)$.
    * *Confusion of the inverse and base-rate fallacy*: these are the common mistakes of confusing $\hat{p}(y \mid x)$ with $\hat{p}(x \mid y)$ or with $\hat{p}(y)$.
    * *Split-sample histograms, ECDFs, and boxplots*: these cut a continuous $\hat{x}$ into groups, then reuse the plots from [Data & Visualization](01_02_Data.qmd) within each group.

```{r}
## MAIN EXAMPLE
# Lab data: 3294 US workers.
# Wages1 has one row per worker and four columns.
data(Wages1, package='Ecdat')

# Pick two of those columns to form a bivariate dataset.
# Schooling is in years, and wages are per hour in 1980 dollars.
xy_hat <- Wages1[, c('school', 'wage')]
colnames(xy_hat) <- c('x_hat', 'y_hat') # x_hat=years of schooling, y_hat=hourly wage
xy_hat[1, ]                             # first worker's two values
```

## Joint Distributions

#### **Discrete Data**{-}

When two variables are recorded together for each observation, the first question is how often each combination of values appears.

:::{.callout-important icon=false title="Key Definition" collapse="false"}
The *joint distribution* of two discrete variables $\hat{x}_{i}$ and $\hat{y}_{i}$ is the table giving the share of observations with $\hat{x}_{i}=x$ and $\hat{y}_{i}=y$, for every combination of values $(x,y)$:
$$\hat{p}(x,y) = \sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathbf{1}\left( \hat{x}_{i}=x, \hat{y}_{i}=y \right)/n,$$
where $\mathbf{1}(\cdot)$ is an *indicator function* that equals $1$ if the expression inside is TRUE and $0$ otherwise.
:::

The joint distribution is also called a *frequency table* (or *cross-tabulation*).
It is useful for summarizing how two categorical variables co-occur, and the other distributions in this chapter are computed from it.
Dividing the count by $n$ puts the cells on a probability scale, so each cell reports a proportion of the sample and the whole table sums to one.

Sometimes we only need to summarize one of the two variables and ignore the other.

:::{.callout-important icon=false title="Key Definition" collapse="false"}
The *marginal distribution* of $\hat{x}_{i}$ is the univariate distribution obtained by summing the joint distribution over all values of $\hat{y}_{i}$.
The marginal distribution of $\hat{y}_{i}$ is obtained by summing the joint distribution over all values of $\hat{x}_{i}$.
$$\hat{p}(x) = \sum_{y} \hat{p}(x,y) \quad \quad \hat{p}(y) = \sum_{x} \hat{p}(x,y).$$
:::

The *marginal* gets its name from the row and column margins of the joint table, where it is usually written.
It is useful for recovering each variable's own distribution from the joint table.
It also supplies the base rates $\hat{p}(x)$ and $\hat{p}(y)$, which conditional distributions divide by.
The same numbers can also be computed directly from the univariate data without ever forming the joint table (see [here](01_06_EstimationTheory.qmd#estimates)).

For example, consider two discrete variables from the lab data.
```{r}
## MAIN EXAMPLE
# All 3294 workers: x=years of schooling, y=sex
school_sex <- Wages1[, c('school', 'sex')]

# Frequency table and joint distribution
tab <- table(school_sex) # raw counts: rows=school, cols=sex
tab
prop <- tab / sum(tab)   # joint sample distribution (sums to 1)
round(prop, 3)
# For example, p(x=12, y=female) is about 0.180.
# So about 18% of workers are women with 12 years of schooling.

# addmargins() appends row and column totals (i.e., the marginals)
prop_m <- addmargins(prop)
round(prop_m, 3)
# The row totals give the marginal of schooling: p(x=12) is about 0.361.
# The column totals give the marginal of sex: p(y=female) is about 0.48.
```

Each cell of the joint table is the share of all observations with that combination of values.
The row totals are the marginal distribution of $\hat{x}_{i}$.
The column totals are the marginal distribution of $\hat{y}_{i}$.

Note that you can compute various univariate statistics using the marginal distributions.
E.g., the mean of $\hat{x}_{i}$ is $\hat{m}_{X}=\sum_{x} x \hat{p}(x)$.
The code below computes it for the above example.
Try computing the standard deviation $\hat{s}_{X}$ yourself.
```{r}
# marginals and univariate statistics
p_x <- margin.table(prop, 1)
sum(p_x * as.numeric(names(p_x)))
mean(school_sex[, 'school'])
# Both ways give a mean of about 11.6 years of schooling.

# p_y <- margin.table(prop, 2)
```

:::{.callout-note icon=false collapse="true" title="Must Know"}
It helps to work through a small table by hand.
Suppose we observe a sample of $n=13$ students with two discrete variables:

* $\hat{x}_{i}$ depicts years of education, taking values in $\{12, 14\}$
* $\hat{y}_{i}$ depicts sex, where $y=1$ means female and $y=0$ means male

Assume the count data are summarized by the following table:

\begin{array}{c|cc}
 & y=0\ (\text{male}) & y=1\ (\text{female})\\
\hline
x=12 & 4 & 3 \\
x=14 & 1 & 5 \\
\hline
\end{array}

The joint distribution divides each cell count by the total number of observations to obtain
\begin{array}{c|cc}
 & y=0 & y=1\\
\hline
x=12 & 4/13 & 3/13 \\
x=14 & 1/13 & 5/13
\end{array}
The marginal distribution of $\hat{x}_{i}$ is
$$\begin{aligned}
\hat{p}(x=12) &= \hat{p}(x=12,y=0) + \hat{p}(x=12,y=1) = \frac{4}{13} + \frac{3}{13} = \frac{7}{13}, \\
\hat{p}(x=14) &= \hat{p}(x=14,y=0) + \hat{p}(x=14,y=1) = \frac{1}{13} + \frac{5}{13} = \frac{6}{13}.
\end{aligned}$$
The marginal distribution of $\hat{y}_{i}$ is
$$\begin{aligned}
\hat{p}(y=0) &= \hat{p}(x=12,y=0) + \hat{p}(x=14,y=0) = \frac{4}{13}  + \frac{1}{13} = \frac{5}{13}, \\
\hat{p}(y=1) &= \hat{p}(x=12,y=1) + \hat{p}(x=14,y=1) = \frac{3}{13}  + \frac{5}{13} = \frac{8}{13} .
\end{aligned}$$

Together, this yields a frequency table with marginals:
$$
\begin{array}{c|cc|c}
 & y=0\ (\text{male}) & y=1\ (\text{female}) & \text{Row total}\\
\hline
x=12 & 4/13 & 3/13 & 7/13\\
x=14 & 1/13 & 5/13 & 6/13\\
\hline
\text{Column total} & 5/13 & 8/13 & 1
\end{array}
$$ {#eq-joint-educ-sex}

The mean of $\hat{x}_{i}$ is $12 \times \frac{7}{13} + 14 \times \frac{6}{13} = \frac{84+84}{13} = \frac{168}{13} \approx 12.9$.

```{r}
# Simple hand-built dataset: 13 students, two variables each
xy0_hat <- rbind(
    c(12, 0), c(12, 0), c(12, 0), c(12, 0), # 4 male with 12 years
    c(14, 0),                                # 1 male with 14 years
    c(12, 1), c(12, 1), c(12, 1),            # 3 female with 12 years
    c(14, 1), c(14, 1), c(14, 1), c(14, 1), c(14, 1)) # 5 female with 14 years
colnames(xy0_hat) <- c('educ', 'female')
xy0_hat <- as.data.frame(xy0_hat)

# Frequency table and joint distribution
tab0  <- table(xy0_hat)      # raw counts: rows=educ, cols=female
prop0 <- tab0 / sum(tab0)    # joint sample distribution (sums to 1)

# addmargins() appends row and column totals (i.e., the marginals)
prop0_m <- addmargins(prop0)
round(prop0_m, 2)

# marginals and univariate statistics
p0_x <- margin.table(prop0, 1)
sum(p0_x * as.numeric(names(p0_x)))
mean(xy0_hat[, 'educ'])
```
:::


#### **Continuous Data**{-}

*Scatterplots* are used frequently to summarize the joint distribution of continuous data.
They can be enhanced in several ways.
As a default, use semi-transparent points so as not to hide any points (and perhaps see if your observations are concentrated anywhere).
You can also add other features that help summarize the relationship.

```{r}
## MAIN EXAMPLE
# With 3294 points, very transparent points keep dense areas readable.
# Schooling is in whole years, so the points form vertical stripes.
plot(y_hat ~ x_hat, xy_hat, pch=16, col=grey(0, .1),
    main=NA, xlab='Years of schooling', ylab='Hourly wage (1980 dollars)')
# The darkest stripe is at 12 years, where workers are most concentrated.
# A few very high wages stretch the vertical axis.
```

You can also show the marginal distributions of each variable along each axis (see this [margin and layout cheatsheet](https://r-graph-gallery.com/74-margin-and-oma-cheatsheet.html) for how `layout()`, `mar`, and `oma` work together).

```{r}
# Setup Plot
layout( matrix(c(2, 0, 1, 3), ncol=2, byrow=TRUE),
    widths=c(9/10, 1/10), heights=c(1/10, 9/10))

# Scatterplot, with limits that line up with the marginal bars below
# The wage axis stops just past 20 dollars, so the 16 largest wages are not drawn.
par(mar=c(4, 4, 1, 1))
plot(y_hat ~ x_hat, xy_hat, pch=16, col=grey(0, .1),
    main=NA, xlab='Years of schooling', ylab='Hourly wage (1980 dollars)',
    xlim=c(2.5, 16.5), ylim=c(0, 20))

# Add Marginals
# Schooling bars are centered on whole years.
par(mar=c(0, 4, 1, 1))
f_x_hat <- hist(xy_hat[, 'x_hat'], breaks=seq(2.5, 16.5, by=1), plot=FALSE)
barplot(f_x_hat[['counts']], axes=FALSE, space=0, border=NA)

# Wage bars span one dollar, and only the 20 bars up to 20 dollars are drawn.
par(mar=c(4, 0, 1, 1))
f_y_hat <- hist(xy_hat[, 'y_hat'], breaks=seq(0, 40, by=1), plot=FALSE)
barplot(f_y_hat[['counts']][1:20], axes=FALSE, space=0, horiz=TRUE, border=NA)
# Schooling piles up at 12 years, and wages have a long right tail.
```

:::{.callout-tip icon=false collapse="true" title="Test Yourself"}
Repeat this figure for the $50$ states in `USArrests`, with urban population on the horizontal axis and murder arrests on the vertical axis.
```{r}
# USArrests has 50 rows (one per US state) and four columns.
# Pick two of those columns to form a bivariate dataset.
xy2_hat <- USArrests[, c('UrbanPop', 'Murder')]
colnames(xy2_hat) <- c('x_hat', 'y_hat') # x_hat=urban population share, y_hat=murder arrests per 100K
xy2_hat[1, ]                             # first state's two values

# Setup Plot
layout( matrix(c(2, 0, 1, 3), ncol=2, byrow=TRUE),
    widths=c(9/10, 1/10), heights=c(1/10, 9/10))

# Scatterplot
par(mar=c(4, 4, 1, 1))
plot(y_hat ~ x_hat, xy2_hat, pch=16, col=grey(0, .5),
    main=NA, xlab='Urban Population', ylab='Murder Arrests')

# Add Marginals
par(mar=c(0, 4, 1, 1))
f_x2_hat <- hist(xy2_hat[, 'x_hat'], plot=FALSE)
barplot(f_x2_hat[['counts']], axes=FALSE, space=0, border=NA)

par(mar=c(4, 0, 1, 1))
f_y2_hat <- hist(xy2_hat[, 'y_hat'], plot=FALSE)
barplot(f_y2_hat[['counts']], axes=FALSE, space=0, horiz=TRUE, border=NA)
```
:::

A two-dimensional histogram summarizes the joint distribution by counting the observations in each rectangle of a grid [@Scott2015].

## Conditional Distributions

#### **Discrete Data**{-}

Often we want to know how the distribution of one variable changes when we restrict attention to a subgroup defined by another.

:::{.callout-important icon=false title="Key Definition" collapse="false"}
The *conditional distribution* of $\hat{y}_{i}$ given $\hat{x}_{i}=x$ is the joint share renormalized so the row at $\hat{x}_{i}=x$ sums to one:
$$\hat{p}(y \mid x) = \frac{\hat{p}(x,y)}{\hat{p}(x)}, \quad \quad \hat{p}(x \mid y) =\frac{\hat{p}(x,y)}{\hat{p}(y)},$$
where $\hat{p}(x)$ is the marginal of $\hat{x}_{i}$ and where $\hat{p}(y)$ is the marginal of $\hat{y}_{i}$.
:::

Conditional distributions are useful when one variable splits the data into meaningful subgroups (sex, education level, treatment status) and we want to compare the outcome distribution across those subgroups.
Dividing by $\hat{p}(x)$ changes the unit of analysis.
Each row now sums to one, so each row is a probability distribution over $y$ for the given $x$.
A cell no longer reports a share of the whole sample.

For example, return to the joint distribution table from the lab data.
To compute the conditional distribution of $\hat{y}_{i}$ given $\hat{x}_{i}=x$, we rescale the numbers in each row so that each row sums to 1.
```{r}
## MAIN EXAMPLE
# Conditional distribution of sex given schooling: each row sums to 1
round(prop.table(tab, 1), 3)
# With 10 years of schooling, about 58% of workers are male and 42% female.
# With 13 years of schooling, about 44% of workers are male and 56% female.
```

We can also compute the conditional distribution of $\hat{x}_{i}$ given $\hat{y}_{i}=y$, $\hat{p}(x \mid y) = \hat{p}(x,y) / \hat{p}(y)$, just as we did above.
In this case, we rescale the numbers in each *column* of the joint distribution table so that each column sums to 1.
```{r}
# Conditional distribution of schooling given sex: each column sums to 1
round(prop.table(tab, 2), 3)
# Among female workers, about 38% have 12 years of schooling.
```

:::{.callout-note icon=false collapse="true" title="Must Know"}
Return to the sample of $n=13$ students and its joint distribution table, @eq-joint-educ-sex.
To compute the conditional distribution of $\hat{y}_{i}$ given $\hat{x}_{i}=x$ by hand, we rescale the numbers in each row so that each row sums to 1.
Specifically, for $x=12$, we compute
$$\begin{aligned}
\hat{p}(y=0 \mid x=12)
&= \frac{\hat{p}(x=12, y=0)}{\hat{p}(x=12)}
= \frac{4/13}{7/13}
= \frac{4}{7} \\
\hat{p}(y=1\mid x=12)
&= \frac{\hat{p}(x=12, y=1)}{\hat{p}(x=12)}
= \frac{3/13}{7/13}
= \frac{3}{7}
\end{aligned}$$
Similarly, for $x=14$, we compute
$$\begin{aligned}
\hat{p}(y=0 \mid x=14)
&= \frac{\hat{p}(x=14, y=0)}{\hat{p}(x=14)}
= \frac{1/13}{6/13}
= \frac{1}{6}. \\
\hat{p}(y=1\mid x=14)
&= \frac{\hat{p}(x=14, y=1)}{\hat{p}(x=14)}
= \frac{5/13}{6/13}
= \frac{5}{6}.
\end{aligned}$$
Together, we find
\begin{array}{c|cc|c}
 & y=0\ (\text{male}) & y=1\ (\text{female}) & \text{Row total}\\
\hline
x=12 & 4/7 & 3/7 & 7/7\\
x=14 & 1/6 & 5/6 & 6/6\\
\hline
\end{array}

In this example, we say that

* conditional on students having $12$ years of education, $4/7$ are male and $3/7$ are female.
* conditional on students having $14$ years of education, $1/6$ are male and $5/6$ are female.
:::

:::{.callout-tip icon=false collapse="true" title="Test Yourself"}
Continuing the $13$-student example above, show that

* among male students, $\approx 80\%$ have 12 years of education.
* among female students, $\approx 38\%$ have 12 years of education.

Try programming the results, especially if you are stuck or uncertain

```{r}
xy0_hat <- rbind(
    c(12, 0), c(12, 0), c(12, 0), c(12, 0), #Male
    c(14, 0), 
    c(12, 1), c(12, 1), c(12, 1),
    c(14, 1), c(14, 1), c(14, 1), c(14, 1), c(14, 1))
colnames(xy0_hat) <- c('educ', 'female')
xy0_hat <- as.data.frame(xy0_hat)

tab0 <- table(xy0_hat)
tab0

# Joint distribution
round(prop.table(tab0), 3)

# Conditional distribution of Y given X
round(prop.table(tab0, 1), 3)

# Conditional distribution of X given Y
round(prop.table(tab0, 2), 3)
```
:::

Different conditional distributions change the unit of analysis.
Swapping which variable is in the denominator like this generally answers a different question.

* $\hat{p}(y=\text{female})$ answers "what fraction of workers are female?"
* $\hat{p}(y=\text{female} \mid x=13)$ answers "what fraction of workers are female within the subgroup with 13 years of schooling?"
* $\hat{p}(x=13 \mid y=\text{female})$ answers "what fraction of workers have 13 years of schooling within the subgroup that is female?"

Confusing the different distributions is so common that they have names.

:::{.callout-important icon=false title="Key Definition" collapse="false"}
The *confusion of the inverse* is the mistake of confusing $\hat{p}(y\mid x)$ with $\hat{p}(x\mid y)$.
The *base-rate fallacy* is the mistake of confusing $\hat{p}(y\mid x)$ with $\hat{p}(y)$.
:::

:::{.callout-note icon=false collapse="true" title="Must Know"}
**Women and education.** Suppose you read that women are more educated than men.
Check the claim against the $13$ students in @eq-joint-educ-sex.
Three statements sound alike but are not.

* "Women are more likely than men to have $14$ years of education."
  This compares the education share *within each sex*: $\hat{p}(x=14 \mid y=1) = 5/8 \approx 0.63$ for women versus $\hat{p}(x=14 \mid y=0) = 1/5 = 0.20$ for men. 
Women are higher by a factor of three.
* "Students with $14$ years of education are mostly women."
  This is the sex share *within the educated group*: $\hat{p}(y=1 \mid x=14) = 5/6 \approx 0.83$.
Women are higher by a factor of five.
* "Most students are women."
  This is the *base rate*: $\hat{p}(y=1) = 8/13 \approx 0.62$.
Women are higher by a factor of less than $2$.

The *confusion of the inverse* is to read the first statement as the second.
Both use the same numerator, the $5$ women with $14$ years of education, but divide by different groups: the $8$ women or the $6$ educated students.
Here, the statements disagree on magnitude: are women $3$ or $5$ times more educated?

The *base-rate fallacy* is to forget that the second statement depends on the third: how many educated students are women depends on how many students are women.
In this sample, most educated students are women ($5/6$) partly because most students are women ($8/13$).
Now imagine the sample had $50$ men instead of $5$, with the same $20\%$ rate.
Then $10$ men and $5$ women would have $14$ years of education: women would still be three times as likely to be educated, yet $\hat{p}(y=1 \mid x=14) = 5/15 = 1/3$, so most educated students would be men.
Rearranging the definition shows where the base rate enters:
$$\begin{aligned}
\hat{p}(y=1 \mid x=14)
&= \frac{\hat{p}(x=14, y=1)}{\hat{p}(x=14)}
= \frac{\hat{p}(x=14 \mid y=1)\,\hat{p}(y=1)}{\hat{p}(x=14 \mid y=0)\,\hat{p}(y=0) + \hat{p}(x=14 \mid y=1)\,\hat{p}(y=1)}.
\end{aligned}$$
The rates within each sex, $5/8$ and $1/5$, are the same in both samples.
Only the base rate $\hat{p}(y=1)$ changed, from $8/13$ to $8/58$, and that alone moved the conditional from $5/6$ to $1/3$.
The Test Yourself examples below repeat this pattern.

```{r}
## MAIN EXAMPLE
# Count table for the 13 students: rows = education, columns = sex
counts <- rbind(
    '12' = c(male=4, female=3),
    '14' = c(male=1, female=5))

# Education share within each sex: p(educ | sex)
round(prop.table(counts, 2), 3)

# Sex share within each education level: p(sex | educ)
round(prop.table(counts, 1), 3)

# Base rate: p(sex)
round(colSums(counts) / sum(counts), 3)

# Same rates within each sex, but 50 men instead of 5
counts_50 <- rbind(
    '12' = c(male=40, female=3),
    '14' = c(male=10, female=5))
round(prop.table(counts_50, 2), 3)     # p(educ | sex) unchanged
round(prop.table(counts_50, 1), 3)     # p(sex | educ) reverses
round(colSums(counts_50) / sum(counts_50), 3)   # base rate p(sex)
```
:::

The base-rate fallacy often shows up as reading a large count as a high rate.
A common category can have the most cases even when its rate per case is the lowest.



:::{.callout-tip icon=false collapse="true" title="Test Yourself"}
**The most-stolen car.** Suppose you read that the Honda Civic is the most-stolen car in a city.
Does that mean a Civic is more likely to be stolen than other cars?
Not necessarily.

Imagine a city with $100{,}000$ cars: $70{,}000$ Civics and $30{,}000$ of other models.
Let $\hat{x}_{i}$ be the model and $\hat{y}_{i}$ whether car $i$ was stolen.
The counts are

\begin{array}{c|cc|c}
 & \text{not stolen} & \text{stolen} & \text{Row total}\\
\hline
\text{Civic} & 69300 & 700 & 70000\\
\text{other} & 29460 & 540 & 30000\\
\hline
\text{Column total} & 98760 & 1240 & 100000
\end{array}

More Civics are stolen than other cars ($700 > 540$), so the Civic is the "most-stolen" model.
But the conditional distributions tell two different stories:

* $\hat{p}(\text{stolen}\mid\text{Civic}) = \frac{700}{70000} = 0.010$ is the theft rate for a Civic.
* $\hat{p}(\text{stolen}\mid\text{other}) = \frac{540}{30000} = 0.018$ is the theft rate for other cars.
* $\hat{p}(\text{Civic}\mid\text{stolen}) = \frac{700}{1240} \approx 0.565$ is the share of stolen cars that are Civics.

A Civic is *less* likely to be stolen ($1.0\%$ vs $1.8\%$), yet most stolen cars are Civics.
The reason is the *base rate*: $\hat{p}(\text{Civic}) = 0.70$ of all cars are Civics.
"Most-stolen" is a statement about $\hat{p}(x\mid y)$ (the model given theft), while car-theft risk is a statement about $\hat{p}(y\mid x)$ (theft given the model).

```{r}
# Count table: rows = model, columns = stolen
counts <- rbind(
    Civic = c(not=69300, stolen=700),
    other = c(not=29460, stolen=540))

# Theft rate by model: p(stolen | model)
counts[, 'stolen'] / rowSums(counts)

# Share of stolen cars by model: p(model | stolen)
counts[, 'stolen'] / sum(counts[, 'stolen'])
```
:::

How far a signal moves $\hat{p}(y\mid x)$ away from $\hat{p}(y)$ depends on the base rate $\hat{p}(y)$ itself.
The fraud-detection example below applies one screen to a rare outcome and then to a common one.

:::{.callout-tip icon=false collapse="true" title="Test Yourself"}
**Fraud detection.** A bank's model flags $99\%$ of fraudulent transactions and $1\%$ of legitimate ones.
What is the chance that a flagged transaction is fraud?
The answer depends on the base rate $\hat{p}(y)$: the share of all transactions that are fraud.

Let $\hat{x}_{i}$ be whether the model flags transaction $i$ and $\hat{y}_{i}$ be whether the transaction is fraud.
Suppose fraud is rare, $100$ of $100{,}000$ transactions, so $\hat{p}(\text{fraud}) = 0.001$.
The counts are

\begin{array}{c|cc|c}
 & \text{legitimate} & \text{fraud} & \text{Row total}\\
\hline
\text{not flagged} & 98901 & 1 & 98902\\
\text{flagged} & 999 & 99 & 1098\\
\hline
\text{Column total} & 99900 & 100 & 100000
\end{array}

Before seeing the model's output, the chance that a transaction is fraud is the base rate, $\hat{p}(\text{fraud}) = 100/100000 = 0.001$.
After seeing a flag, it is the conditional, $\hat{p}(\text{fraud}\mid\text{flagged}) = 99/1098 \approx 0.09$.
The flag matters: it raises the chance of fraud $90$-fold.
But $91\%$ of flags are still false alarms, because the $1\%$ false alarm rate applies to $99{,}900$ legitimate transactions, which swamps the $99$ true detections.

Now suppose fraud is common, $10{,}000$ of $100{,}000$ transactions, so $\hat{p}(\text{fraud}) = 0.10$.
The model is unchanged, but the counts become

\begin{array}{c|cc|c}
 & \text{legitimate} & \text{fraud} & \text{Row total}\\
\hline
\text{not flagged} & 89100 & 100 & 89200\\
\text{flagged} & 900 & 9900 & 10800\\
\hline
\text{Column total} & 90000 & 10000 & 100000
\end{array}

and $\hat{p}(\text{fraud}\mid\text{flagged}) = 9900/10800 \approx 0.92$.
The same flag from the same model means fraud is unlikely in one setting and likely in the other.
The only thing that changed is the base rate.

The base-rate fallacy is to judge the flag by the model's accuracy alone, as if $\hat{p}(y\mid x)$ did not depend on $\hat{p}(y)$.
When the outcome is rare, even an accurate screen produces mostly false positives.
The same arithmetic applies to medical tests for rare diseases, polygraph screening of employees, and airport security checks.

```{r}
# Rare fraud: rows = model output, columns = transaction type
counts_rare <- rbind(
    not_flagged = c(legitimate=98901, fraud=1),
    flagged = c(legitimate=999, fraud=99))
colSums(counts_rare) / sum(counts_rare)      # base rate p(y)
round(prop.table(counts_rare, 1), 3)         # conditional p(y | x)

# Common fraud: same model, base rate 100 times higher
counts_common <- rbind(
    not_flagged = c(legitimate=89100, fraud=100),
    flagged = c(legitimate=900, fraud=9900))
colSums(counts_common) / sum(counts_common)
round(prop.table(counts_common, 1), 3)
```
:::

#### **Continuous Data**{-}

Conditional distributions describe the relationship between $\hat{y}_{i}$ and $\hat{x}_{i}$.
We show how $\hat{y}$ changes according to $\hat{x}$ using a [histogram](01_02_Data.qmd#histogram-density) or bar plot.
When $\hat{x}$ is continuous, as it often is, or takes many values, we split it into distinct bins and convert it to a factor variable.
E.g.,

```{r}
## MAIN EXAMPLE
# Split Data by Years of Schooling above/below mean
# Schooling takes many values, so we bin it like a continuous variable.
m_x_hat <- mean(xy_hat[, 'x_hat'])
m_x_hat
# The mean is about 11.63, so the split falls between 11 and 12 years.
low_school <- xy_hat[, 'x_hat'] <= m_x_hat
y1_hat <- xy_hat[low_school, 'y_hat']  # hourly wages, 11 or fewer years
y2_hat <- xy_hat[!low_school, 'y_hat'] # hourly wages, 12 or more years
cols <- c(low=rgb(.8, 0, 0, .75), high=rgb(0, 0, .8, .75))

# Common Histogram
# One-dollar bins cover every wage.
# The axis stops just past 20 dollars, so the 16 largest wages are not drawn.
ylim <- c(0, .2)
xlim <- c(0, 20)
xbks <- seq(0, 40, by=1)

par(mfrow=c(1, 2))
hist(y1_hat,
    breaks=xbks, col=cols[1],
    main=NA,
    xlab='Hourly wage (1980 dollars)', freq=FALSE,
    border=NA, ylim=ylim, xlim=xlim)
title('Schooling <= Mean', font.main=1)
# Raw Observations (quiet=TRUE skips the warning about wages off the axis)
rug(y1_hat, col=grey(0, .1), quiet=TRUE)

hist(y2_hat,
    breaks=xbks, col=cols[2],
    main=NA,
    xlab='Hourly wage (1980 dollars)', freq=FALSE,
    border=NA, ylim=ylim, xlim=xlim)
title('Schooling > Mean', font.main=1)
rug(y2_hat, col=grey(0, .1), quiet=TRUE)
# Both histograms have a long right tail.
# The group with 12 or more years has more of its wages at higher values.
```

It is sometimes preferable to show the [ECDF](01_02_Data.qmd#empirical-cumulative-distribution-function) instead.
And you can glue various combinations together to convey more information all at once

```{r}
## MAIN EXAMPLE
layout( t(c(1, 2, 2)))
# Full Sample Density
# The axis stops just past 20 dollars, so the 16 largest wages are not drawn.
hist(xy_hat[, 'y_hat'],
    main=NA,
    xlab='Hourly wage (1980 dollars)',
    breaks=xbks, xlim=xlim, freq=FALSE, border=NA)
title('Full Sample Density', font.main=1)
rug(xy_hat[, 'y_hat'], col=grey(0, .1), quiet=TRUE)

# Split Sample Distribution Comparison
# Each curve has over a thousand steps, so draw lines rather than points.
F1_hat <- ecdf(y1_hat)
plot(F1_hat, col=cols[1],
    lwd=2, verticals=TRUE, do.points=FALSE, col.01line=NA,
    xlim=xlim, xlab='Hourly wage (1980 dollars)', ylab='Proportion of workers',
    main=NA, bty='n')
title('Split Sample Distributions', font.main=1)
F2_hat <- ecdf(y2_hat)
plot(F2_hat, add=TRUE, col=cols[2],
    lwd=2, verticals=TRUE, do.points=FALSE, col.01line=NA)

legend('bottomright', col=cols,
    lwd=2, bty='n', inset=c(0, .1),
    title='Years of schooling',
    legend=c('Low (<= Mean)', 'High (> Mean)'))
# The curve for 12 or more years sits to the right over the whole range shown.
# So its higher wages are not driven by a few workers.
```

[Boxplots](01_02_Data.qmd#boxplots) summarize the same two groups side by side.

```{r}
## MAIN EXAMPLE
# Boxplots for the low and high schooling groups
# The axis stops just past 20 dollars, so the 16 largest wages are not drawn.
med_cols <- adjustcolor(cols, alpha.f=2, red.f=.5, green.f=.5, blue.f=.5) # darker shades, for the medians
boxplot(y1_hat, y2_hat,
    names=c('Low (<= Mean)', 'High (> Mean)'),
    main=NA, col=cols, border=NA, medcol=med_cols, ylim=c(0, 20),
    whisklty=0, staplelty=0, outline=FALSE,
    varwidth=TRUE, #show number of obs. per group
    xlab='Years of schooling', ylab='Hourly wage (1980 dollars)')
# Raw Observations, in place of whiskers and outliers
stripchart(list(y1_hat, y2_hat),
    pch='-', col=grey(0, .2), cex=1,
    vert=TRUE, add=TRUE)
# The median and both quartiles are higher for 12 or more years.
```

Boxplots are better suited for conditioning on multiple levels.

:::{.callout-note icon=false collapse="true" title="Must Know"}
You can also split data into more than two groups.
Here we cut $\hat{x}$ into $K=4$ bins and draw one boxplot per bin.
It helps to check how many observations fall in each bin, since evenly spaced bins can be nearly empty.

```{r}
# Here x_hat is years of schooling.
# K Groups with even spacing (not even counts)
K <- 4
table(cut(xy_hat[, 'x_hat'], K))
# Even spacing leaves only 22 workers in the lowest bin.
# It also puts 2248 workers in one bin, including everyone with 12 years.

# K Groups with even counts
quantile(xy_hat[, 'x_hat'], probs=c(.25, .5, .75))
# Even counts are not possible either.
# The median and the third quartile are both 12, so those two breaks coincide.

# K Groups with breaks chosen by hand, about as even as whole years allow
x_cut_hat <- cut(xy_hat[, 'x_hat'], breaks=c(0, 10, 11, 12, 16),
    labels=c('<11', '11', '12', '>12'))
table(x_cut_hat)

# Boxplots for each group
# The axis stops just past 20 dollars, so the 16 largest wages are not drawn.
Kcols <- hcl.colors(K, alpha=.5)
Kmed_cols <- adjustcolor(Kcols, alpha.f=2, red.f=.5, green.f=.5, blue.f=.5) # darker shades, for the medians
boxplot(xy_hat[, 'y_hat'] ~ x_cut_hat,
    main=NA, col=Kcols, border=NA, medcol=Kmed_cols, ylim=c(0, 20),
    whisklty=0, staplelty=0, outline=FALSE,
    varwidth=TRUE, #show number of obs. per group
    xlab='Years of schooling', ylab='Hourly wage (1980 dollars)')
# Raw Observations, in place of whiskers and outliers
stripchart(xy_hat[, 'y_hat'] ~ x_cut_hat,
    pch='-', col=grey(0, .2), cex=1,
    vert=TRUE, add=TRUE)
# The median wage rises from each bin to the next.
```
:::

:::{.callout-tip icon=false collapse="true" title="Test Yourself"}
Repeat these comparisons for the $50$ states in `USArrests`, with murder arrests split by urban population.
Start with one histogram for the states at or below the mean urban population and one for the states above it.

```{r}
# USArrests has 50 rows (one per US state) and four columns.
# Pick two of those columns to form a bivariate dataset.
xy2_hat <- USArrests[, c('UrbanPop', 'Murder')]
colnames(xy2_hat) <- c('x_hat', 'y_hat') # x_hat=urban population share, y_hat=murder arrests per 100K

# Split Data by Urban Population above/below mean
m_x2_hat <- mean(xy2_hat[, 'x_hat'])
low_urban <- xy2_hat[, 'x_hat'] <= m_x2_hat
murder1_hat <- xy2_hat[low_urban, 'y_hat']  # murder arrests, low urban population
murder2_hat <- xy2_hat[!low_urban, 'y_hat'] # murder arrests, high urban population
cols2 <- c(low=rgb(.8, 0, 0, .75), high=rgb(0, 0, .8, .75))

# Common Histogram
ylim2 <- c(0, .25)
xbks2 <- seq(min(xy2_hat[, 'y_hat'])-1, max(xy2_hat[, 'y_hat'])+1, by=1)

par(mfrow=c(1, 2))
hist(murder1_hat,
    breaks=xbks2, col=cols2[1],
    main=NA,
    xlab='Murder Arrests', freq=FALSE,
    border=NA, ylim=ylim2)
title('Urban Pop <= Mean', font.main=1)
# Raw Observations
rug(murder1_hat, col=grey(0, .5))

hist(murder2_hat,
    breaks=xbks2, col=cols2[2],
    main=NA,
    xlab='Murder Arrests', freq=FALSE,
    border=NA, ylim=ylim2)
title('Urban Pop > Mean', font.main=1)
rug(murder2_hat, col=grey(0, .5))
```

Next, compare the full sample density with the ECDF of each group.

```{r}
layout( t(c(1, 2, 2)))
# Full Sample Density
hist(xy2_hat[, 'y_hat'],
    main=NA,
    xlab='Murder Arrests',
    breaks=xbks2, freq=FALSE, border=NA)
title('Full Sample Density', font.main=1)
rug(xy2_hat[, 'y_hat'], col=grey(0, .5))

# Split Sample Distribution Comparison
F_lowpop_hat <- ecdf(murder1_hat)
plot(F_lowpop_hat, col=cols2[1],
    pch=16, xlab='Murder Arrests',
    main=NA, bty='n')
title('Split Sample Distributions', font.main=1)
F_highpop_hat <- ecdf(murder2_hat)
plot(F_highpop_hat, add=TRUE, col=cols2[2], pch=16)

legend('bottomright', col=cols2,
    pch=16, bty='n', inset=c(0, .1),
    title='% Urban Pop.',
    legend=c('Low (<= Mean)', 'High (> Mean)'))
```

Then compare the same two groups with boxplots.

```{r}
# Boxplots for the low and high urban population groups
med_cols2 <- adjustcolor(cols2, alpha.f=2, red.f=.5, green.f=.5, blue.f=.5) # darker shades, for the medians
boxplot(murder1_hat, murder2_hat,
    names=c('Low (<= Mean)', 'High (> Mean)'),
    main=NA, col=cols2, border=NA, medcol=med_cols2,
    whisklty=0, staplelty=0, outline=FALSE,
    varwidth=TRUE, #show number of obs. per group
    xlab='% Urban Pop.', ylab='Murder Arrests')
# Raw Observations, in place of whiskers and outliers
stripchart(list(murder1_hat, murder2_hat),
    pch='-', col=grey(0, .5), cex=2,
    vert=TRUE, add=TRUE)
```

Finally, cut urban population into $K=4$ evenly spaced bins and draw one boxplot per bin.

```{r}
# K Groups with even spacing (not even counts)
K2 <- 4
x2_cut_hat <- cut(xy2_hat[, 'x_hat'], K2)
table(x2_cut_hat)

# Boxplots for each group
Kcols2 <- hcl.colors(K2, alpha=.5)
Kmed_cols2 <- adjustcolor(Kcols2, alpha.f=2, red.f=.5, green.f=.5, blue.f=.5) # darker shades, for the medians
boxplot(xy2_hat[, 'y_hat'] ~ x2_cut_hat,
    main=NA, col=Kcols2, border=NA, medcol=Kmed_cols2,
    whisklty=0, staplelty=0, outline=FALSE,
    varwidth=TRUE, #show number of obs. per group
    xlab='Urban Population', ylab='Murder Arrests')
# Raw Observations, in place of whiskers and outliers
stripchart(xy2_hat[, 'y_hat'] ~ x2_cut_hat,
    pch='-', col=grey(0, .5), cex=2,
    vert=TRUE, add=TRUE)

# 4 Groups with equal numbers of observations
#Qcuts <- c(
#    '0%'=min(xy2_hat[, 'x_hat'])-10*.Machine[['double.eps']],
#    quantile(xy2_hat[, 'x_hat'], probs=c(.25, .5, .75, 1)))
#x2_qcut_hat <- cut(xy2_hat[, 'x_hat'], Qcuts)
#boxplot(xy2_hat[, 'y_hat'] ~ x2_qcut_hat, col=hcl.colors(4, alpha=.5))
```

## Exercises

1. Comment the script you wrote for this chapter, then restart R and check that it runs from a clean session, then check the script with AI as explained in [Working with AI](04_A_WorkingWithAI.qmd).
   Write three sentences from memory on the main statistical idea of this chapter, and ask the assistant what is wrong, vague, or missing.
   Finish with your own questions about whatever you found hardest.

2. Explain the difference between a joint distribution, a marginal distribution, and a conditional distribution.
   Using the schooling-and-sex example from this chapter, describe in words what $\hat{p}(y=\text{female} \mid x=13)$ tells you and how it differs from $\hat{p}(x=13 \mid y=\text{female})$.

3. Suppose you observe a sample of $n=20$ people with two discrete variables: $\hat{x}_{i}$ takes values in $\{A, B\}$ and $\hat{y}_{i}$ takes values in $\{1, 2\}$.
   The counts are: $(A,1)=6$, $(A,2)=4$, $(B,1)=3$, $(B,2)=7$.
   Compute the joint distribution $\hat{p}(x,y)$, both marginal distributions, and the conditional distribution $\hat{p}(y \mid x)$.

4. Using the `USArrests` dataset, split the variable `Assault` into two groups based on whether `UrbanPop` is above or below its median.
   Plot overlapping histograms of `Assault` for both groups with semi-transparent colors.
   Then plot the ECDF for each group on the same axes with a legend.

#### **Further Reading** {-}

* <https://www.econometrics-with-r.org/2-1-random-variables-and-probability-distributions.html> -- joint, marginal, and conditional distributions in an econometrics context.
* <https://r-graph-gallery.com/histogram.html> -- gallery of histogram styles in R, useful for building marginal-distribution plots.
* <https://www.khanacademy.org/math/statistics-probability/random-variables-stats-library/random-variables-discrete/v/valid-discrete-probability-distribution-examples> -- short video introduction to discrete probability distributions and joint tables.

#### **Recall** {-}

We summarized two variables with joint, marginal, and conditional distributions.
In the `Wages1` schooling-and-sex table, $\hat{p}(y=\text{female}\mid x=13)\approx 0.56$ is the share of female workers *within* the 13-years-of-school subgroup.
We then saw how the base-rate fallacy reads a large count as a high rate (the "most-stolen car" calculation, where Civics are the most-stolen model but *less* likely to be stolen per car).
